speechtext: There is a point of order to be raised in connection with the introduction of this bill because if it proposes that a charge shall be made upon the revenue, it would be out of order.

The answer to the interrogation is obvious. While I have not had any communication direct, the position of this government was stated by me on February 16. If hon. members will refer to page 2151 of Hansard, they will see that my answer to a similar question was as follows:
The only conditions which this government has at any time laid down with respect to direct relief have been to define direct relief as consisting of food, fuel, clothing and shelter or the equivalent thereof, and that there shall be no discrimination in the granting of relief to any applicant by reason of political, racial, religious or other considerations. No limit has ever been set by this government to the amount of relief which shall be granted to any applicant, this being constitutionally a matter wholly within the determination and judgment of the local authorities. It will also be obvious to members of the house that, even aside from the constitutional aspect, such matters are properly for the local authorities to determine.

tenance, then the matter will promptly be considered by the government and such appropriation made as to take up the difference between what those primarily responsible are able to do and the total amount.

speechtext: Generally speaking, the Excise Act is one of the acts which the mounted police are charged to enforce, but the customs department has also a staff of men who to some extent take part in the same work. In provinces where agreements have been made with the provincial authorities the mounted police are also charged with the enforcement of the provincial liquor acts. That does not apply in Ontario, Quebec or British Columbia.

I noticed in the Montreal papers a few weeks ago an account of the seizing of a still in that city, about which complaint had been made for a considerable time past, but about which it is said the mounted police had failed to accomplish anything until after the customs officials had stepped in. I quote from the Montreal Herald of January 19, 1933:
It is believed that the Department of Justice at Ottawa, following many complaints took the matter in hand and ordered special investigators to work under the orders of the collector of customs in Montreal.
Even the lawyer for the accused appeared surprised yesterday when he appeared for police bail for his clients.

The still was then in operation on the same premises the officers raided about noon yesterday.

The rule as to quoting of opinions of people outside the house with respect to matters under discussion seems to be so clear that we should not have any difficulty in interpreting it when the house makes its own rules to govern its own conduct. To introduce the 246th member by quoting in the house the opinion of someone not in the house with respect to a matter not under discussion is to add to the membership of the house an irresponsible outsider. That is clear, as I understand the rule. Certainly in England it is not done; wherever else it may be done it is not done there.
It has been suggested I have been an offender in this regard myself. I think we all have been. But, with the multiplicity of magazines and papers, and with the number of articles appearing in newspapers for which there is no warrant, does it not occur to the house that in its own interests it should limit the debate to statements of fact made by the members themselves upon their honour as members, after satisfying themselves that those statements are correct, rather than reading statements made by the correspondent of a newspaper, and then stating that "from such and such a paper I read so and so" and ask the house to believe it is true, because someone has said it is true. In my judgment that is not correct practice.

But there are certain limitations to this right, for it is not allowable to read any petition referring to debates in the house, and where the language of the document is such as would be unparliamentary, if spoken in debate, it cannot be read. No language can be orderly in a quotation which would be disorderly if spoken. Nor can any portion of a speech, made in the same session, be read from a private book or paper. It is also irregular to read extracts from newspapers or documents referring to debates in the house in the same session. (May 326.) In making extracts a member must be careful to confine himself to those which are pertinent to the question; it is not regular to quote a whole essay or pamphlet of a general character.
I wonder if the hon. gentleman is reading the whole essay or pamphlet!
Neither is it regular for a member to read a paper which he is asking the house to order to be produced.
This is not produced.
Nor is it in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or other communications, whether printed or written, emanating from persons outside the house, and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member, or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
There is a reference to English Hansard:
"Allusion to debates in the other house are out of order," says May, "and there are few orders more important than this for the conduct of debate and for observing courtesy between houses."
Then Bourinot continues:
During a debate on the tariff in the session of 1877, Mr. Mills referred to the opinions of Sir Alexander Galt, formerly a member and Minister of Finance. Subsequently one of the Canadian papers published a letter from Sir Alexander in answer to some of Mr. Mills' remarks; and the latter rose and proposed reading from the paper in question: but the Speaker interrupted him and questioned the propriety of this course,

a decision entirely in accordance with the English rules of debate. It is in order, however, for a member to quote from a printed paper, on which he proposes to found a motion.
The same thing should be said about a question he asks.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to disagree with some of the general statements made by the right hon.
[The Chairman.]
Prime Minister. I do disagree with you, sir, and the assertion that there is any rule in the book of rules of this house or the customs of this house that would justify a ruling along the lines that you indicated you might give.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no set rule.

Exactly,
there is no such rule. Therefore any statement by yourself, Mr. Chairman, in connection with this point would be your opinion as to the proper conduct of this house. You would in that way be establishing a precedent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. member
will allow me, the chairman has to go by the well-known maxim stare decisis. He must be guided by the previous decisions of the speaker or chairman which have been voted upon by the house.

I think the chairman would be well-advised to be guided by the procedure which is customary in the British house also. I think he hardly did justice to his own well-read mind when he said it was not the custom in the British house to give quotations. Anyone who has studied the British Hansard recently will find numerous quotations. I recall for example that Sir Robert Home in the budget debate last year quoted from Allison's History of Rome very freely in connection with certain monetary questions-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It was written before
the debate.
Time after time t/he right hon. leader of the government has attempted to influence the opinion of the house by quoting-
The new despotism!

-in support of his own opinion from Salter to Gladstone and Bryce and heaven knows who. It is almost impertinence on the part of any hon. member at this stage in the development of parliamentary procedure to suggest that because it is inconvenient or unpleasant for him to listen he should wipe out the customs of the past. This house has established definitely the custom within certain limits of relevancy or appropriateness of quoting authorities, sometimes of value, sometimes of little value, depending on whose opinion it is. There is also the practice in connection with the estimates, I have noted for over eleven years, of quoting from newspapers and asking questions based thereon. The only way we can get information in connection with affairs with which we are not personally acquainted

Supply-Justice-Mounted. Police
is from newspapers. To correct items in newspapers we must ask questions in regard thereto. I have no knowledge of the newspaper item that brought about this discussion, but I think the subject matter of it justifies questions based thereon,-not charges but questions to the minister. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that you will reconsider your decision and not make a brand new rule of your own to go down in history as one of the most serious curtailments of free speech and public opinion that this house has been subjected to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I gather
from the temper of the committee that this discussion bids fair to be protracted. It is of course, perfectly competent to the committee to debate this item at great length, if it chooses to, but may I point out respectfully that, as was indicated by the Minister of Justice, all that this item does is to release funds which have been paid by the provinces into consolidated revenue, and make them available for the use of the service within this fiscal year. And unless my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) would be prejudiced by the delay may I point out that he would have ample opportunity to discuss any point arising with respect to the mounted police in the main estimates. I would like to have these estimates passed at an early date. I do not suggest for one moment that it is not competent to the committee to discuss this item as long as it chooses, but inasmuch as there will be ample opportunity in connection with the main estimates, I suggest that that might ease us over the difficulty for the moment.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has
already spoken on the point of order.

I think I may be
granted a word in reply to the Minister of Finance.

But this is the
point of order-

The hon. member has

May I point out,
Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister spoke twice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am endeavouring to
give a fair decision, but at the same time I cannot ask hon. members to follow the rules 53719-197
strictly if I do not follow them myself. The leader of the opposition wishes to speak to the point of order. I desired in the meantime to read the article and I asked the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to be good enough to let me see it, but he would not let me have it. Obviously therefore he puts me in a difficult position. In the meantime I must give the floor to the leader of the opposition on the point of order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I hope it will not be necessary for the chairman to give a ruling. It need not be necessary if what, sitting here, I heard was correct. It seems to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the chairman are at cross purposes. The statement of the article which the hon. member was attempting to read has been denied. What the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said-at least as I heard him-was that the article which he wished to read, if not true, should be denied.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Should be quoted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. I did not understand the hon. member to say that the statement it contained was correct. What he did say was that if it were not correct it should be denied, and I heard the Prime Minister himself say that it was not correct. The Prime Minister himself denied it. It seems to me that if that is the situation there is no need for any ruling at all. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has asked the ministry a question with respect to a certain statement that appears in the press but which does not bear any relation to this debate, because this debate has commenced only to-day whereas the article in question was printed some time ago. It is perfectly proper for him, when the house is discussing estimates of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to ask any question with relation to the mounted police and to ascertain whether or not a statement referring to the police is correct. I think that was what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was doing. He read a certain article with a view to ascertaining whether it was correct or not. He did not himself say whether it was correct or not. If it was correct it was a serious reflection on the mounted police and therefore he thought we ought to discuss the matter; but if it was not correct, he said it should be denied. If the minister denies that the statement is correct that settles the matter without the necessity for any ruling whatever. Certainly, if the chairman takes a different view-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The chairman expressed no opinion. He asked to see the article to see for himself whether it was relevant and applicable to this debate, but the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre refused to let him have it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It could not possibly be a comment on this debate inasmuch as this debate started only this afternoon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Would it shorten matters, Mr. Chairman, if I were to say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the two articles have been brought to my attention by the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and that they are not correct?

May I offer a suggestion, Mr. Chairman. Some time ago the same point came up that we are discussing this afternoon and you decided that certain articles could not then be read. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The feeling of the house on that occasion did not change my opinion.
But does not the action of the House of Commons on that occasion constitute a precedent which should guide the chairman of committees or the Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would, if it had been a decision. Had the house given a decision I should be bound by it. What did occur on that occasion was this. I said that if the house seemed to be unanimous against me I would not press my decision.
But you were convinced, Mr. Chairman, that the house was unanimous against your decision.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

That is not the way parliament has been conducted heretofore.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wished to prevent the hon. gentleman from being stopped while he was reading the article.
With due respect to you, Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to submit articles to you in order that I may know whether or not I may read them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

No; I do not propose to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

In the eleven years that I have been in this house we have never had to submit articles to the chairman before attempting to read them, and I do not propose to do so to-day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was doing it as a matter of courtesy to the hon. gentleman, but he can go on.

I appreciate the
courtesy but I decline to accept it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

No, I do not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I am not raising the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I was reading an article that had been brought to my attention, conveying the information that although the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had been informed with regard to the existence of a still they had not succeeded in unearthing it nor in making the arrest.

I rise to a point of order. A few minutes ago the Minister of Justice

denied the statement with regard to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police having made an investigation, and in answer to the hon. member he said that the information contained in the article was not true. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is now persisting in his statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has the right to accept a denial made by any other hon. member with respect to facts personal to himself, but he can state any fact that he knows of, or has heard of or that has been published in the press, notwithstanding the denial of any other hon. member. I am therefore willing, so far as this debate is concerned, to let him proceed with his statement of facts.

Hasn't the point been decided, Mr. Chairman? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has endeavoured to read an article which, I understand, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice have denied, and that ought to settle that point. But may I point out that so far as the article in question is concerned, as the leader of the opposition has indicated, it could not possibly refer to any proceeding that had taken place in this house. This is clear from paragraph 306, which reads:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
It could not be said that this article is expressing an opinion or is reflecting upon the proceedings within the house because the matter has just originated. The whole thing should be dismissed at once. The statement has been denied and it must be accepted and besides it has no bearing upon the proceedings of the house, as the right hon. leader of the opposition has pointed out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Simply to read an
article does not mean that it must be accepted. Surely the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) cannot ask me to decide this matter without my seeing or having heard read the article in question.

I cannot conceive of any proceeding in this house whereby a member is asked to submit an article from a newspaper or anything of that kind to the Speaker or the Chairman before it is read.
53719-197i

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I agree with that. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has the floor.
What item are we dealing with?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 394.

I will content myself at the moment with asking a definite question of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie). Is it true that efforts were made about January 19 by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to locate a still which they were unable to do and that later on instructions were given to the collector of customs who succeeded in locating the still and having the men arrested and the still destroyed? If we can get back to the original matter, I should like to inquire if there is close cooperation between these two groups of officials. If this article is true and if the customs officials had to be sent out after a futile investigation by the mounted police, it would reflect upon the efficiency of the mounted police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can only repeat what
I stated before. Both these newspaper articles were brought to my attention by the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who informed me that the statements contained therein were not correct. There are two forces in Montreal, one belonging to the customs department and called the customs investigation branch and the other, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The customs investigation branch claims certain rights and privileges in regard to these matters. It has been said that when seizures are made they are allowed part of the fine or penalty whereas the mounted police are not. There was some friction between the two bodies, but that has ceased. The new commissioner has been in Montreal and the various jurisdictions have been established. The articles which have been read in part by the hon. member are not correct and place an entirely untrue light upon the whole situation.

Grant to the Pacific Science Association towards expenses of the fifth Pacific Science Congress, $70,000.
Where is this meeting to take place?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This was arranged for before we came into office.

I should like to know who and what is the Pacific Science Association?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only information I have is that this vote is necessary as a result of an invitation extended by the preceding government to the Pacific Science Association which held its last meeting in Java in 1929. As to the details of the character of the organization and the subjects which it studies, I would have to ask that that explanation be given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) who is not here at the moment. I find that I have not these details before me.
Seventy thousand dollars is a great deal of money to vote just "as is" and I suggest that we should have some information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps I can assist the hon. gentleman. Canada has been represented at various meetings of this organization which comprises most of the countries which border upon the Pacific ocean. The last meeting was held in Java. We have extended invitations, I think twice, to the congress to meet in Canada but until the 1929 meeting our invitations were not accepted. We then became obligated as hosts to this organization. Owing to economic conditions, the meeting which was set for last year was postponed, but it became clear that it could not be postponed again. This organization discharges rather important functions with respect to various matters- the circumstance that it met in Java in 1929 is some indication of that fact-and it deals with scientific problems of the first order connected with various matters which arise in the Pacific area. I do not think any of us are anxious that we should spend this money but, on the other hand, this country occupies rather an important place in international matters and the invitation has been extended and accepted. I understand the meeting is to be held in Vancouver. There is no sum less than this vote that we could arrive at which would enable the matter to be dealt with properly. Doctor Tory has given a great deal of attention to the matter and various scientific organizations in the country are interested. Unless we become "welchers" we are not warranted in refusing to pass this vote. That is not a very excellent term to use, but it expresses exactly the true situation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
May I say that I am happy to be able to agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). As I recall it, this organization is one of the world scientific organizations. It deals more particularly with problems relating to the Pacific and Canada, being a country that borders on the Pacific, is deeply interested in the study

and research carried on. As the Prime Minister has said, Canada has .been represented at previous meetings. Our representatives have been entertained1 by other countries and the turn of Canada had come to invite these other nations to our country. In doing so it was thought that we were not only performing an international courtesy but also doing something that would .be of real advantage to Canada itself.

We have heard from two of the most able men in Canada but both of them have failed to give us any real information as to the purposes of this body. One said that as they met in Java last year, that would give an indication of the scientific importance of this organization. I do not know very much about Java. I associate that country only with coffee and I do not know what scientific bearing the fact that this organization met in that country would have. The leader of the opposition is also vague in his remarks; he says that it is of great scientific importance. Would somebody, if he knows, tell me what was discussed at Java and is now to be discussed at Vancouver? Has it to do with the marine life of the Pacific or with trade or what? I am quite willing to vote the money; I do not want, as the Prime Minister suggested, to be a welcher, but I should like to know what we are voting and what we are getting out of this affair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am bound to say that
the members of the organization comprise some of the most eminent scientists of the world. I am afraid, if I were to read one of their papers, it would not add greatly to the sum total of the knowledge of more than a few members of the house.

It would be ruled out
of order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It would not be out
of order, because it would be merely a statement in answer to a question as to what was done at the meeting. I have not brought with me a copy of the proceedings at the last meeting. As a matter of fact I thought probably the committee would be content with an explanation of the circumstances under which we are called upon to make the expenditure in question. I promise the hon. gentleman between now and the consideration of the estimates of some department, say External Affairs, I shall endeavour to bring down the last volume and perhaps make it available for him so that he may be able to add to the sum total of his knowledge.

Supply-Miscellaneous

How many delegates are
expected at this congress?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am speaking subject
to correction, but I think 100 eminent scientists gathered at the meeting in Java. The Japanese meeting was more largely attended. It is expected that probably 100 scientists will attend the meeting at Vancouver.

For a meeting of 100
scientists, it is necessary to vote $70,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may say that the Japanese government, during the period this organization met there, expended $250,000 and the cost to Java was some $130,000, so that it will be observed that the sum we ask as compared with those figures is rather modest.
How are the expenses allocated between the different countries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A committee of Canadian scientists under the chairmanship, if my memory serves me aright, of Doctor Tory, has accepted the responsibility of preparing for the meeting and making the necessary arrangements, shall I say on a very meagre scale as compared with what was done at the last two meetings, to try to provide for the meeting in a way that will not be unworthy of Canada. The committee is not at the moment large, but I think additions have been made to the number. If my memory serves me correctly-and I speak subject to memory-there is a small local committee that Doctor Tory established at Vancouver in the course of a recent visit to that city. Last year the work was proceeding with a good deal of difficulty when it was concluded, with the consent of the organization. that the meeting would be postponed until jthis year. I would not like those who come here to read this debate as an indication of the welcome that will be extended to them if they come to this country.

Grant to Philip Campbell re illegal warfare claim, $1,460.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may say that this particular item is not to be classed with those cases which may be considered Canadian and which were dealt with by the reparations commission. The facts of the case, as I recall them, are that this man was a member of the crew of a British trawler. He was for a time interned in Germany with his associates who were members of the crew. After the war he became a resident of Australia and in 1921 or
thereabouts he moved to Canada. He was in this country for some time before he discovered that his associates had all been reimbursed by the British government. He put his claim into the Canadian reparations commission and very properly in the circumstances it could not be granted. Then representations were made to the Imperial authorities who would have granted compensation as was done in the case of his shipmates, but unfortunately he made his application after the cases had been closed in the mother country and it was impossible for him to receive compensation. So the British government said this: Inasmuch as we have compensated a number of Canadians without calling upon Canada to pay, we think, as a matter of courtesy and of fairness in the circumstances, you might be able to take care of this man who now has a residence in Canada. So, as a matter of grace, we felt in these circumstances that to place this man upon a parity with his shipmates, we should ask for this particular appropriation. In view of the conditions of to-day, the cost of living, the value of the pound sterling and the comparable amounts which were paid to his shipmates in England, I think the figure in this item is rather high, and I am going to ask my deskmate to move that the sum be reduced by $160. I think the compensation of $1,000 is reasonable.

That is compensation in
full?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and it is admitted it is purely a case of a compassionate grant.
It is not a legal claim?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Who fixed the amount at
$1,460?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Due to exchange, I think
there was an error in the figures. Who prepared them, I cannot say. In the ordinary course the supplementary estimates come to my office and I do not examine them until they are presented to my colleagues in council. As a matter of fact the item came into the estimates at the instance of the Department of External Affairs after communication with the home authorities.
Has Philip Campbell returned to his home in the old country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, he is a resident of
Canada to-day.
What amount was paid by the British government to his shipmates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister Without Portfolio

I move that the item be reduced in the sum of S460.

organized districts, public health in other districts, Tracadie and Bentinck island Lazaret-toes and leprosy generally, $162,000.

I would like to get some
information from the minister respecting the appointment of a medical superintendent at the lazaretto at Tracadie. What I desire to learn is whether a permanent appointment of a medical superintendent has yet been made; who is temporarily in charge, and when does the minister expect a permanent appointment will be made.

speakeroldname: Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The appointment of the medical superintendent at Tracadie lazaretto has not yet been made. The medical officer who is temporarily in charge at Tracadie during the vacancy is Doctor Peloquin, a medical officer of the

Department of National Health. He has had experience in dealing with leprosy at our lazaretto on the Pacific coast. The position I understand is now being advertised by the Civil Service Commission.
May I ask if Doctor Hache of Caraquet was not placed in temporary charge in October last? If so, what position does he now occupy in connection with the lazaretto.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Doctor Hache was in charge for a certain time; I do not recall the exact months, but he is not associated with the lazaretto at the present time.

The minister has just stated that the vacancy is now being advertised by the Civil Service Commission. Is it not a fact that it was advertised last year and that applications were received, that Doctor Hache was one of the applicants among others, and that no action w'as taken by the Civil Service Commission at that time towards making a permanent appointment? If that is so, why is the position advertised a second time?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think the statement by the hon. member for Gloucester is correct, so far as I heard him. Doctor Hache was temporarily acting, but has not been appointed.
What about the first call for applicants by the Civil Service Commission? Why was there a second call?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Because his appointment was not confirmed.

But there were other applicants? Why the necessity for a second call for applicants, when there were three or four other applications from medical men, men who had undergone the so-called examination, and some of whom were returned soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I cannot answer that, because it is a matter which comes under the control of the Civil Service Commission. They decided the position would be advertised for, but I do not know anything beyond that. I am not familiar with their special reasons.

I say the committee has a right to know those special reasons. I do not say the minister should carry them in his mind, but at least he should endeavour to obtain them. In practice, it is very seldom indeed that the Civil Service Commission call for a second tender-if I may use that term-without having received some intimation from the department. Here we have a

Supply-National Health
vacancy created by the retirement on pension of Doctor J. A.Langis, the man who for twenty or twenty-five years was in charge of the lazaretto. He was perfectly willing to accept his superannuation, but had to be replaced. The vacancy was advertised. A number of physicians, some of whom I know to be very capable men, applied for the position. As I have already said some were returned soldiers. Yet the appointment has not been made. Although almost a year has passed the appointment has not been permanently made, and the commission make a second call for applicants. There must be some reason for it, and I believe the committee is entitled to know what the reason is, if the minister can possibly get it from the commission. We are entitled to know why the applicants in the first instance are all thrown aside and new applications asked for. I am convinced it is not fair to the men who applied at first, and especially unfair to the returned soldiers.
Although I represent Gloucester county, through illness in the last six months I have been unable to keep in touch with my constituents. Until the minister announced it to-day I was not aware that Doctor Peloquin was temporarily in charge. I understood Doctor Hadhe was still in charge. Further, I was not aware that the Civil Service Commission had made a second call, and was greatly surprised to learn it. I contend we are treating those men unfairly who were called upon to go through the usual routine the Civil Service Commission requires in such cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I cannot speak for the Civil Service Commission. I know what they have done; they have decided to advertise again, and all I can say to the hon. member is that I do not believe any previous applicant has been treated unjustly, because his application will be in order now just as it was previously.

It cannot be in order. If I had learned of these circumstances before I left home, and had not been surprised by receiving the information to-day, I would be in a better position to speak. I claim an injustice has been done Doctor Hache. He will not have the same standing before the Civil Service Commission upon his second application that he had on his first. Doctor Hache was placed in charge of the lazaretto on October 2, 1932; the minister himself placed him in charge. Then the minister made a tour through Gloucester county, and when going through my home town was kind enough to call upon me. I believe the minister's call
was just at the time Doctor Hache was placed in charge. However, the date makes no difference. Doctor Hache and the minister, when on their way to Tracadie, called upon me at my home, and upon that occasion the minister informed me he was going to instal Doctor Hache temporarily. I was very happy to see that an appointee from the county of Gloucester was to be placed in charge of the hospital; I did not consider the matter from a political standpoint at all. I felt the work rightfully belonged to a doctor from the county of Gloucester providing he could qualify. Doctor Hache has been temporarily in charge of the hospital at Tracadie. He resides at Caraquet, a distance of twenty-one miles from the institution, and visits it three times a week, which was all he was called upon to do. I understand he was paid according to the services rendered; in other words he was not paid a full-time salary, but was paid a proportion of the full salary paid previously to the resignation of Doctor Langis.
Doctor Hache has been set aside. Is it because his services were not satisfactory? Was Doctor Peloquin called in to take charge of the lazaretto because it was found that, after serving three or four months Doctor Hache's services were not satisfactory to the department. Action certainly would not be taken through the Civil Service Commission because before they could act they would have to get a report of his qualifications as a temporaiy employee from the department. I claim what has taken place is a reflection on Doctor Hache, and that he does not stand the same chance on a second application or examination as he did on the first. He has been replaced, and an official permanently employed who is at the disposal of the department to be sent here and there for relief work, and to relieve superintendents in medical institutions. I claim that the department must have had some reason for taking that action. Having had some reason, they must report it to the Civil Service Commission, if Doctor Hache applies a second time. If he does apply a second time, whatever reason the department may give will militate against him. I claim the regular appointment should have been made when the Civil Service Commission received the applications and were in a position to decide upon the qualifications of each applicant. In five or six months they should not turn around and say, "We will call for new applications." What they should have done was to place Doctor Hache aside as a temporary employee and place Doctor Peloquin in charge temporarily. Then the Civil Service Commission could
Supply-National Health

have gone on with the applicants they had and made an appointment, instead of waiting until nearly a year after and then calling for new applications.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
As the hon. member
for Gloucester says, they might have, but they did not. The Civil Service Commission act for themselves, I cannot speak for them.

Who displaced Doctor
Hache?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have stated to the
committee that his temporary appointment was not confirmed by the Civil Service Commission.
Who replaced him as a temporary officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Excuse me if I finish
what I am saying. I would like to correct a minor point in the statement of the hon. member for Gloucester. I did not say to him that I went down to instal him, because Doctor Hache had been attending there previous to my arrival in Bathurst.
Just two days.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Well if it was one day. So it was not an installation. His appointment was on temporaiy certificate of the Civil Service Commission, not by the minister or the department.

I would like to broach a matter that comes under this item. There has been established in Toronto and Winnipeg and possibly other cities throughout Canada, sponsored by the provincial governments with the aid of the federal government, depots or offices for the interception and treatment of venereal disease. These offices have done splendid work, so much so that the discoverable incidence of this disease has been diminished fifty per cent in a comparatively short time. This year and last year and the year before no provision was made bj the federal authorities for this grant, and the province of Manitoba at least was forced to discontinue the service. In view of the very far spread1 incidence of this form of disease-and it is impossible to find an adjective which describes the devastating effect it has on society and the people of the country at large-I would like to plead with the Minister of Health that he would try and find a means of placing an item in the estimates that would enable this work to be carried on in the province of Manitoba. It would1 not only be a charitable work but a work for the protection and welfare of the whole nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will
bring the views of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) concerning this matter to the attention of the government. I would not like to give any answer now, but I will be pleased to bring the matter before my colleagues. I notice he asks that this amount be available for the treatment of venereal disease in the province of Manitoba. I think probably it would have been better had the request been made to apply generally, as before.
Quite so, but I am from Manitoba.

I would like to ask the
minister how many stations there are in Canada where leprosy is being treated, and where they are located?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
There are two lazarettos in Canada, one on the Atlantic and one on the Pacific. The one at Tracadie, New Brunswick, is much the older institution, because leprosy became endemic there, it had its home there, in fact I think that is the only instance in Canada where leprosy has become seated among the people. It has diminished very considerably as years go on. I visited the lazaretto there something like thirty or forty years ago and there were about thirty cases, and all of them had developed within that area. To-day there is a total of ten cases. But it does not mean that these cases arose in the east of Canada or the neighbourhood of Tracadie. It has now become a hospital for oases of leprosy found to exist over the eastern half of Canada. There are comparatively few of the ten that came from the original source about Tracadie. That is an instance where leprosy has diminished slowly but very substantially.
The other lazaretto is at Bentinck island, Williams Head, Vancouver island. It is a small island near Vancouver island. There are five cases of leprosy there to-day. All are Chinese. In fact the history in western Canada has been that the cases of leprosy are largely Chinese. These Chinamen are sent back to their home, if possible, but in a number of cases it is not possible on account of transportation reasons.
Has scientific medicine developed to a point where a permanent cure can be effected?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Leprosy is essentially
a long standing disease, usually very slow in progress. Certain cases come to a finality, apparently they are cured. No doubt they are assisted by treatment, but time is also

Supply-National Health
an important element. There are cases of leprosy that do not tend to progress, even apart from any special treatment. On the whole treatment is of value, it certainly relieves, it extends their lives and makes them more comfortable. The treatment is not a prompt curative agent, but is of value all the same. As I say some cases become quiescent and are apparently cured.

How many cases
are there at Tracadie?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Ten in Tracadie,
Gloucester county, New Brunswick, and now five at Bentinck island, Williams Head, British Columbia.
Are the ten cases at Tracadie members of the white face?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Hon. members can
easily understand bow occasionally a case creeps into Canada. Most recently a case was found of a British subject, white, who had lived in South America and subsequently came to Canada. That was a case which no doubt originated in South America. They are all white, and there are a few from the neighbourhood and others from various parts who have come to Canada and afterwards shown the disease. There is one patient who is supposed to have become infected in South Africa. Naturally a case creeps in occasionally, as I say. There is a general impression that leprosy is a highly contagious disease, but that is not the case. It is contagious, it is true, because that is the explanation of its continuing all through the ages; but with proper care and attention, proper living, it is only slightly so. If, however, people live in one household and do not take care of themselves-it is pretty much the same in the case of tuberculosis-then the disease is conveyed. In the case of the lazaretto at Tracadie, the institution is in charge of a community of sisters. That community has been there for very many years, and no case of leprosy has developed among any of the sisters. This is a good opportunity, I think, of indicating the excellent care that the sisters show, the proper spirit, and the kindness which they exhibit in their work. They are devoting their lives to the care of these lepers.

I wish to
add a word in support of the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Boniface, that it is the grave duty, particularly under present conditions, that the Dominion government and its department of health should interest themselves directly, both financially and otherwise, in the growing problem of venereal disease throughout the country. It is not
necessary for me to tell the minister that under conditions of unemployment and underemployment, and under conditions of reduced income on the part of many of the middle and lower classes, there is a pressure which is greater than ever on the provincial clinics which have been maintained with some success-considerable success in many provinces. That strain, as the minister knows, has been very heavy owing to the fact that hundreds of people who formerly could afford to undertake private medical treatment now make application to the clinics, being unable to defray the cost privately. In view of the general conditions resulting from this state of affairs, and the conditions that will continue to result from want of adequate care of these cases, I would urge upon the minister that he give serious consideration to the proposal of the hon. member for St. Boniface, in the hope that next year if not this year there will be a large vote from this department for their responsibility in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I shall keep the matter
before me.

The minister did not give
me the date that Doctor Peloquin was temporarily in charge at Tracadie.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have not the date
here.

Will the minister obtain it
for me and let me have it by communication?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I certainly will.

How long has the lazaretto been in existence at Tracadie, what was the greatest number of patients afflicted with leprosy at any one time, and at what date? I gather from what the minister has said, and I believe it to be the fact, that there has been a diminution in the number of cases in Canada in recent years and that the disease is now regarded as controllable, from the point of view of preventing any contagion to attendants. I should like to know how long ago the institution was established and when it had the greatest number of patients; also how that number compares with the number to-day. I take it that the patients in British Columbia come practically entirely from boats and largely from the orient. That was the impression I gathered, and I also gathered that no new cases have broken out there among residents in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I should not care to give the exact date as to how long ago the lazaretto was established there. There has been more than one in that neighbourhood. I think how-
Supply-National Health

ever it goes back to 1830; it may be 1844, I am not quite sure. There has been a diminution in the number of patients, but as I said a few moments ago most of the cases now there are cases that are sent from the eastern half of Canada, and they are not Canadian cases because they have not developed in Canada; they have just drifted in. Actually there are now very few so called Canadian cases that have developed in this country. The Chinese come from abroad; in fact, most of the cases in Tracadie have come from abroad. There are a few however that originated in the area I speak of, where the lazaretto now is, and that is the explanation of the lazaretto being there. In the British North America Act there is a section providing that one of the duties of the federal government shall be to provide and care for lepers in Canada.
What was the greatest number at any one time in Canada, and when?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am informed that the greatest number at any one time in Tracadie was twenty-eight. I think there were quite that number there in 1886.
And the number in Tracadie now is between nine and eleven?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The total number of
cases at Tracadie is ten, but I do not think that more than two or three are natives of New Brunswick. The others are from large centres like Toronto and Montreal.

In the past lepers have
been received at Tracadie hospital from the British WTest Indies. I think we have had one or two Chinamen and also some Icelanders. Leprosy was first discovered in Gloucester county some eighty or ninety years ago. It was supposed to have been brought in by a ship-wrecked crew. That was before confederation and before the federal government took over the care of lepers, this service was provided by the province. At that time the lepers were stationed at Sheldrake island on Miramichi bay. They became somewhat disgruntled and revolted and burned dowm the establishment. After confederation the federal government took charge and a colony was established on the western shore of Tracadie harbour. In 1887 the government made a grant and the present lazaretto was constructed. At that time the occupants of this colony were mostly residents of Gloucester county but I am pleased to be able to say that leprosy has been almost entirely eradicated from this district. This has been brought about by medical treatment 
and the watchfulness upon the part of the officials of the federal government in following up suspected cases and, despite opposition, placing them in the lazaretto. As the minister has said, at the present time there are about ten inhabitants in the lazaretto and of that number, not more than two or three are natives of Gloucester. These are old people who have been in there for years. There have been cases of absolute cure. I know of one old lady who was declared to be cured. She lived outside the lazaretto for years but finally asked that she be allowed to return there in order that she might die in the place where she had received such wonderful care. The sisters were employed after the federal government took charge and have had charge of this colony ever since. This old lady to whom I refer had been a resident in the lazaretto for some twenty-five or thirty years but due to recent medical discoveries, a perfect cure had been effected. I am informed that there are other cases now in the lazaretto well on the road to absolute recovery.

If there are only five
cases in the institution in British Columbia, all from the orient, why could not they be deported or moved east in order that the institution could be closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think I indicated the reason a short time ago. With one exception, we have returned all that it was possible to return. Difficulty is placed against the return of the other inhabitants by the transportation company. If a man happens to be disfigured 6r his hands or face ulcerated to any great extent, it is not possible to have the shipping company accept him for transportation to China. There is one man who might be returned but he has been found to be very useful in looking after the others and making them comfortable.
Could not they be moved east? Surely the difficulties of transportation could be surmounted.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is natural for one
to ask why these people should not be sent back to their country of origin, but I hope I have explained the difficulties in the way. It would be very desirable if that could be done but due to the attitude taken by the shipping companies it has been found impossible to do so.

Why not move them
east and close the western institution? That would save some S80,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Would it? This is a
question about which one has to know a good

Supply-National Health
deal before he can offer an opinion. How much does the hon. member think it would cost to transport a leper from British Columbia to Tracadie? Such transportation would involve a special car as neither the Canadian Pacific nor the Canadian National will allow such a case even in a drawing-room which is quite separate from the rest of the car and believed to be absolutely safe. But the fact is that they will not do so. This means there has to be an attendant. As hon. members seem to be really very much interested in this matter, let me give them our experience of the last case we sent to Tracadie. It will cost about $700 to send that one case there from Toronto. We have to be a little cautious about advocating economy on those rates. If you bring those five cases from the coast and place them in Tracadie, what guarantee is there that next week there will not be another case, because they are liable to occur anywhere in Canada amongst the Chinese, and then the same process has to be repeated? The department was carrying on prior to my time-and I am not taking any credit for this-and is continuing to act in the wisest, sanest and most economical manner possible.

I know there was an
agitation some years ago to have all the lepers in Canada put in one place, and I think those in charge thought a certain quarantine station at Grosse Isle would be a suitable place. When you talk of sending lepers to any particular spot, you will find no enthusiasm on the part of the people of that district. I happen to know because I was in charge of that department at the time somebody suggested that being done and I quite agree with what the minister has said in regard to the inadvisability of attempting to move a patient affected with this disease either any great distance or from one station to another where there has not hitherto been a hospital for this kind of patient. It is a matter of great satisfaction to those in charge of the department from time to time that this disease is gradually diminishing and that the fear of contracting it is nothing like as great to-day as it was, say, twenty-five or thirty years ago. I do not think any good purpose will be served by attempting to move the patients who are now in Vancouver to Tracadie or any other place.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Just to complete this
subject, I should like to say that opinions vary in reference to the care of lepers. Everyone is agreed that under ordinary circumstances this disease is not contagious to any substantial extent. For instance, of all the sisters at Tracadie with all their contact, nursing, dressing wounds, and so forth, not
one has contracted the disease. That is because they are careful and understand the matter. Recently letters have come to the department from quite an outstanding physician stating that we were too strict about this matter and that the act was too severe in calling upon those cases to go to a lazaretto. First, let me say that nearly all of the cases that I have seen in Canada, with perhaps one exception, are of poor people and they must be cared for in some way; second, if a subject of leprosy is able to care for himself in the way of a home and nursing, it seems to me that the most practical thing to do is to allow him to go to the lazaretto. Such a patient will have somebody with whom to associate, the opportunity of gardening, boating, fishing and be able to live in a more wholesome, natural and happy manner than if allowed to remain in some other place where the public would have fear of the disease.

I should like to make a further observation on this appropriation. It is true that in the constitution of this country provision has been made for the care of lepers, but that constitution was framed nearly a hundred years ago. I should like to ask the Minister of Pensions and National Health whether he does not consider that there are other infectious diseases of a venereal nature which are much more important to the Canadian people in this day than the incidence of leprosy. I have been a medical man for thirty years in reasonably active practice and I have never come across a case of leprosy, but I should like to state to the minister that I find syphilis in about every tenth patient. This is a matter of vital importance to the Canadian people, and I have no hesitation in making that statement on the floor of the house. The vast majority of people never see leprosy; it is not a very important matter. I would not for a moment have the government of this country ignore it or not make for it the provision that they do, but I say without hesitation that so far as the health of the Canadian people is concerned, the discovery, cure and prevention of syphilis are infinitely more vital matters. There are couples who have married and raised large families of, say, six or seven children w'ho have grown up imbeciles or something of the kind, and it is a fact that neither the parents nor anyone else realized that the trouble was due to this disease. This has been discovered probably only when it was too late to do anybody any good and possibly when the disease might have spread indefinitely. If the government of Canada feels disposed to curtail and, if possible, destroy infectious
Supply-National Health

diseases which threaten the health of the nation, the provinces are reaching out their hands for a little help in order to take the best and most efficacious steps that can be taken. The best we can do so far is to institute clinics. We have had two or three clinics which did splendid work in Canada until suddenly, almost overnight, the assistance from the federal government was shut off.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It was not a sudden, but a gradual reduction.

Well, it did not take very long to put an end to the grant. It has been ended for years although it was for a work that has not been exceeded in importance in this country. I desire again to urge the minister to confer with his colleagues in the cabinet in order that this matter may be seriously considered and that some assistance may be extended to the provinces so that we may once more, if possible, institute these venereal clinics.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend fully appreciates the difference between the two diseases. Leprosy is an obligation of the Dominion government to take care of.
If the Dominion government had known as much about syphilis as about leprosy, that would have been a dominion obligation too.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Please allow me to finish. We had no option in the matter. We did it in the case of leprosy because it was there for us to do, but venereal disease is not an obligation of the federal government. That is the difference.
It should be an obligation of the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The federal government made a grant, which was at one time very considerable, to assist in the treatment of venereal disease. That grant has gradually been decreased, but the grant was made originally to help the movement get on its feet. There is no obligation for us to continue. The cases are fundamentally different, but I quite sympathize with my hon. friend in the views he has put forward, and I shall bring them to the attention of my colleagues.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which might not strictly be considered a federal matter, but rather provincial, but yet I think the federal authorities would have at least some interest in it seeing that these items come under the heading of national health and the particular item we are dealing with deals with

public health in other districts, among other things. The matter I wish to mention is the length of hours which nurses are obliged to work in taking care of the sick. I know that it is a provincial matter but I think it is worthy of being brought to the attention of the Minister of National Health. Our nurses in the various hospitals throughout the country are required to work twelve hours a day, from seven in the morning to seven in the evening, and the night shift from seven in the evening to seven in the morning, often with scarcely enough time to grab their meals while they are working. I have been connected with a hospital for several years, sitting on the board, and I have often wondered why our provinces do not take action and reduce the working hours of the nurses. Surely the health of these nurses should be considered. They have no labour organization like our masculine sex has to present their pleas and petitions even on the floor of this house, and try and get reasonable working hours. Generally speaking, men do not work more than eight hours a day, but here are young girls plodding away for twelve hours a day, and by so doing many of them ruin their health and prematurely shorten their days. Seeing that this comes under national health, I wonder if the minister would not think it worth while taking the matter up with the provinces, through the provincial departments of health, with a view to having the hours which the nurses are required to work brought down from twelve to, say, possibly eight hours a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That is primarily a
matter for the provinces. The question of the number of hours a day they should work would raise a very difficult question no matter under what authority it comes. Hosiptal orderlies of course, work similar hours, as well as that splendid branch of humanity, the medical men., although I am not making a personal reference there. The hours can hardly be avoided, but I may say for the comfort of my hon. friend that I appreciate what the nurses have to do, the long hours they have to work, and their faithful services, but in the majority of instances I believe that they have many opportunities to sit down and rest during their period of duty. It is not a continuous occupation like that of a girl in a factory.
I should like first of all to have some helpful suggestion from my hon. friend. It is a matter that is brought to our attention frequently, although it is hardly in our field, but that of course does not prevent us taking a proper interest in the subject. Just at the moment I do not see any solution.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Supply-National Health
Immigration medical inspection, $141,500.

Would the minister tell the committee why the expenditure is still so high? I understood that immigration had been reduced most materially and that the offices abroad had been closed, but here we are spending $141,500 for medical services in connection with immigration. Do we still keep a staff of doctors in England or where are these doctors who are being paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The amount does seem considerable in view of the fact that immigration has been reduced so very greatly, but still it will be noticed that there is a decrease in the expenditure from last year, and the figures for the last few years, which I expect to have in a moment, will show a similar reduction. No matter how small the immigration, it is necessary to maintain a certain organization at the various seaports; in this country, at Halifax and Saint John, Quebec, Montreal and in the west. Then in Europe we have a medical office in London, with two medical officers, and one at Liverpool, Glasgow, Belfast, Paris, Hamburg and Antwerp, together with stenographic staffs. In 1928-29 we had twenty-nine medical officers overseas as compared with eight to-day, a reduction of twenty-one, and that of course means a material reduction in the expenditure. In the year 1931-32 the total expenditure in Canada, Great Britain and the continent was $178,947.13. That is as against $162,000 this year. In the year 1930-31 the total expense was $254,160.10. That shows a substantial reduction. If hon. members wish, I could give the items to show how that amount is made up. The estimates for this year for these medical officers and their staffs are as follows:
Salaries, $85,433.50.
Allowances, including clothing, $10,000.
Wages, $1,000.
Professional services, $1,000.
Equipment and supplies, $15,000.
Rent, $9,000.
Travelling and incidental expenses, $14,000.
Miscellaneous, $6,006.
Or a total of about $141,500.

While I
have no complaint with regard to the reduction in immigration explained by the minister, I do think that in view of the statements by this government to the effect that it intends very seriously and drastically to limit migration to this country under present conditions, there is not a valid excuse for an expenditure of $140,000 for medical inspection. I believe those offices at Antwerp and in European countries generally, outside of Great Britain, should all be closed. I strongly recommend
to the minister that the closing of all European offices outside of those in Great Britain would be a great step in the direction of cleaning this matter up.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That has not been overlooked by the department. The advice of the immigration department is asked concerning the number of medical officers who should be in Great Britain and on the continent. Within the last twelve months there has been a reduction of twenty-one medical officers. That is evidence of withdrawing with considerable speed. At the present time we have only one man in Paris, one in Hamburg and one in Antwerp. I am advised by the Department of Immigration that that is a minimum number which we should have at those points. Then, there are two in London, one in Liverpool, one in Glasgow and one in Belfast. That is a very small number, even with immigration where it is to-day. As we have come down to only eight officials on the continent and in Great Britain, hon. members must realize that the saving is very material. These medical officers are paid between $3,000 and $4,000 a year, with the addition of some living allowance. Therefore I believe I can assure the hon. member for Bow River that the matter is being considered from a practical standpoint, and staffs are being steadily cut down.
Has there been any reduction in the staff in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
There has been a small reduction; I may be in a position to give the figures later. The number employed is in proportion to the amount of work required to be done. There are always ships coming in to Halifax and Saint John. For that reason there must be officers at those points. During the' summer months they come to Quebec, and provision must be made at that point.
While in the year 1931-32 we had forty men on the staff that number has been reduced by nine.

I note from the
report of the Department of Immigration and Colonization for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1932, that there were only 7,332 British immigrants from the British Isles and 4,123 from all other countries, other than the United States. That would mean that there were only between 11,000 and 12,000 immigrants, and it would seem to me that the staffs are still too large to handle only that number of people. Further, if the staffs on the other side are doing their work effectively it seems strange to me that we should still have a total rejection of 324 at ocean
Supply-National Health

ports for the fiscal year 1931-32. Would the minister explain why it is necessary to have so many people to handle so few immigrants, and if they are well handled on the other side why there are so many rejections on this side.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I would suggest the
number is very small. We have only four in the British Isles. People sail from many ports, and, if we have immigrants examined by our own medical men, I do not believe we could get along with a smaller number of officials. Were the 324 immigrants mentioned by the hon. member all coming to Canada?

I have given the
figures appearing in the report showing rejections at ocean ports, nationality and sex, for the fiscal year 1931-32.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Let me say that all
immigrants who come to Canada have not necessarily been previously examined. Those coming from Great Britain, and the parts of the continent I have mentioned, are examined. But, for instance, those coming from Norway, Sweden, or Denmark are not examined, and when they come to Canada a larger proportion of these are refused admission.

speechtext:

Britain two Canadian medical officers-
On the continent.

speechtext:

the number of examinations, there has been a marked reduction. In 1929-30 they numbered 131,185; in 1930-31, 62,975; in 1931-32, 16,958. This year, with incomplete figures it is estimated that there will be 6,000 examinations.

examinations made?

speechtext: I cannot give the points I am merely mentioning our own medical officers.

How many examinations did
the man at Hamburg make?

speechtext: I am sorry, but I have not the figures here.

I can hardly see the possibility of an examiner at Paris doing all the work for the southern part of Europe. If he cannot, of what use is he to this dominion? Do immigrants coming from Russia have to come to Antwerp or Hamburg to be examined, or does the medical examiner go to certain ports to examine?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I cannot give the figures.
What medical examination or inspection is made of American immigrants coming into this country, and where are they examined?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: As far as I know there is no difference in the examination. They are passed by the medical men as they come through.
Where are they examined?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are seen by the medical officer, and if he is satisfied he lets them come through.

Have we Canadian medical examiners at the line to examine them as they come through? I have never seen any. I have been at Canadian ports when immigrants were coming through and I have never seen any Canadian doctor or anyone else examine them. In my constituency a man who some time ago came into this country from the United States developed in the last few years an incurable disease and is a charge

Supply-National Health
on the municipality. I think it is the duty of the federal government to examine immigrants; if they are negligent, or have no medical examiner it is up to them to look after the patient, not leave it to the municipality.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The system followed by the Canadian authorities is the same as that followed in the United States. While they are not actually examined, if there is a suspected case the immigrant is detained for examination by the medical officer. But examiners are not posted all along the border, either by us or by the Americans.

I wish to lodge a protest. Where an immigrant comes into Canada from the United States and is accepted by the immigration authorities, and subsequently develops an incurable disease and becomes a charge on the municipality, the government should either have him deported or take care of the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The hon. member understands, of course, that if a man is in such a condition that he should be deported, he can be sent back.

I would call the attention of the minister to the case of a great war veteran in my riding. This is a non-political matter and I think it is deserving of the attention of parliament. Last fall I brought to the attention of the minister the fact that this man was not receiving the attention he deserved from the pension board, and which he asked for two years ago. He was an early volunteer, a Belgian by birth having his domicile in Canada. At Valcartier he was inoculated, and following inoculation one arm became useless and has been useless ever since. Owing to this bad arm he had no active service overseas. When he was discharged he went on his farm in the Porcupine district and there for sixteen consecutive years carried on the work of a pioneer settler and farmer, never asking any help from the government. But two years ago, after putting up this long struggle, he realized that he could not support his family on his holding, and he then made application to the pension board to have his arm examined. Last fall, when I brought that matter to his attention, the minister was kind enough to refer it to the board. Under the orders of the pension board Private Hussin was sent to the Christie
street hospital in Toronto-that was the second time. There his trouble was diagnosed as hysterical paralysis. He was discharged as cured of this ailment and returned to his holding, and after trying to carry on for a number of months he was unable to support himself and had to receive relief. Throughout that time he has suffered untold misery and has had great difficulty in keeping his family. Now, I have every confidence in the medical men, but I may tell the minister that in my section of the country we strongly resent the conclusion reached by the medical board as a result of their examinations. The man undoubtedly suffered from the electrical treatment he received when he went to Christie street. I would ask hon. members to read the editorial articles that have appeared in connection with this case in the Porcupine Advance, as well as articles published in the Globe, and they will see that what I have said is fully corroborated by these newspapers. They urge, not so much upon the government as upon the Board of Pension Commissioners, the reopening of the case.
It is really a sad spectacle, and although I am a poor man I w'ould gladly pay the travelling expenses of this unfortunate ex-soldier to have him brought before a committee of this house so that the medical men and the members here could see for themselves just what his condition is, because there is no doubt whatever that the man is absolutely helpless. He is entirely without the use of one arm and is utterly unable to get employment in the mines, nor is he able to work on his own farm. I have no hesitation in mentioning these facts because I think it is important for the house to have the information. I know the minister is sympathetic to the case, as will be seen in the fact that only last fall he found it advisable to send the man back to Christie street hospital.
I repeat, I would gladly pay all expenses of this man in order to have him appear before a committee of the house. If hon members could see him they would agree with me that he is not a hypocrite; he is not playacting but is actually a cripple. To send him back to Christie street would be a crime. He is afraid of the treatment he received there, and he knows from past experience that he cannot be cured of his present ailment.

I would point out to the hon. member that at Christie street hospital they have all the means of making a thorough examination, and after going fully into the case they made their diagnosis.
