The diagnosis was
wrong; I defy anyone to dispute that. We are intelligent people in our section of the country and we are convinced that this man has not received fair treatment. It is therefore my bounden duty to present the case to the committee. I know that within the four corners of the act there was room for fair treatment of this man's case. The people in my part of the country are of the opinion that we should have the whole list of pensions paid to the war veterans. I do not think we shall get it, but it seems that because this man has been able to carry on for a number of years the medical board has come to the conclusion that he is not entitled to consideration. That is why I protest against the treatment he has received, and I appeal to the fair-mindedness of this house whether it is not simple justice to have the case reopened so that this man may receive the pension he deserves.
I can assure the minister that the case is not by any means settled so far as the people in that section of the country are concerned. This man is entitled to fair treatment. He enlisted in the war and gave his services to the country and, I say, it is my duty to bring his case before 'parliament. I know that the Minister of Health has been trying to deal fairly with these cases, but I must tell him in all frankness that we are not satisfied with the present situation so far as this case is concerned. Some remedy should be found for this man's condition. I have sufficient confidence in the Board of Pension Commissioners and in the minister himself to believe that this matter will be taken up again, not in two or three years' time, not in two or three months, but immediately. If the minister wants the newspaper articles to which I have referred I will send them to him, just as I did last fall. Strong editorials have appeared in the Porcupine Advance, an independent Conservative newspaper which has taken up this question. That newspaper has discussed matters pertaining to northern Ontario and has always kept its articles on a high level. It does not play politics, and there is certainly no room for politics in this particular matter. It is one in regard to which the house should be properly seized of the facts.
Hon. members may say that this is only an individual case, but I would remind them that individuals make up the collective community. I know that some veterans who have not suffered nearly so much as this man have received compensation from the board, and were entitled to it. We are satisfied that they
[Mr. Stanley.!
should have received the compensation they were given, but it is our opinion that there should be a general rule applicable to all alike. And this applies more forcibly to the case I have just brought to the attention of the minister.
There is one more case which I wish to deal with on this occasion. I refer to private H. H. Joanisse, of Cochrane. He appealed to the board a few months ago but his appeal was rejected last January. This returned soldier went overseas and is now suffering from a heart attack. He has also defective eyesight and this makes it impossible for him to engage in any remunerative occupation. I plead now with the minister to acquaint himself with all the facts in connection with these two cases, because, I -cannot repeat it too often, it is my solemn duty to bring these matters to the attention of the house so that these men may receive that treatment to which they are entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I recall fairly well the case referred to by the hon. gentleman; it has been declared to be a case of hysterical paralysis. Apparently the hon. gentleman disagrees with that diagnosis, but that is the considered opinion of the medical examiners. However, I shall ask to have the whole matter reinvestigated, but I do not wish my hon. friend or others to consider that appeals should be taken to the minister to have these matters put right. That is not the province of the minister, nor is it in his power; and I do not know that it is desirable that it should be. It is a matter that rests with the pension board, the tribunal, and the pensions appeal court. They are independent bodies. They were created so with a special object in view, namely, that they should be free to form their own opinions and not be influenced by others. That is the position, and I fancy that when my hon. friend thinks it over he will agree that he is taking fairly strong ground when he suggests that all these medical men are wrong and he is right. There is of course always a possibility of error, but as I recall it, this case was sent to Christie street hospital; an examination was made by a large number of medical men, and there it was the consensus of opinion that it was hysterical and not actual paralysis. I cannot say anything more about the matter, but I will ask that it be again gone into. I repeat, however, that I do not wish this to be interpreted as an opinion on my part that they were wrong or anything of that kind; on the contrary I know that the matter has been carefully studied for a considerable period.

Supply-Pensions

I want to add another word. I am prepared to make the statement outside parliament that in this case the doctors were wrong. In the first place, they were not unanimous in their diagnosis. One doctor, indeed, reported that the condition of the man was pitiful, and the final word of the Board of Pension Commissioners was that he was suffering from hysterical paralysis. The diagnosis has now been changed to that of malingering. They have no right to make such a statement in connection with this man. There is no hypocrisy about him and he was not trying to malinger. I do not understand why that was said about this man. Surely parliament shoud be able to deal with this matter if these doctors or the commission cannot. Considerable dissatisfaction has been caused in my section of the country by this judgment. I am not a medical man but I know it would be impossible for Private Hussin to do any work. That would be impossible because one of his arms is absolutely helpless. Five hundred doctors could not make me think that that man can use his arm. There was no need to use the word "malingering."
Oh, oh.

Some hon. members may think it is all right to laugh, but they have the full use of their limbs and are enjoying good health. This is no laughing matter to a man who enlisted and has been suffering for years. This man was vaccinated and inoculated; by that medical action he practically lost the use of one arm, making it impossible for him to provide bread, clothing and shelter for himself and his family. As far as I am concerned, I feel it to be my duty to bring this situation before the house as often and as forcibly as I can. I repeat that I am prepared to pay the expenses of Private Hussin so that he may appear before any committee of this house when the medical men and members of the house can then see that he is unfit to do any manual work and should receive a reasonable pension.

The minister stated a few minutes ago that he himself did not have any power in these cases because tribunals had been established in Canada to deal with pension applications. I desire to take this opportunity of drawing to the minister's attention five outstanding pension cases which do not come within the category of the reply made by the minister to the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette). I should like to refer to the
repoi't of the committee appointed to investigate into the administration of the Pension Act and to quote the findings of at least a section of that committee in regard to these cases. This section of the report is signed by General Ross, Mr. Myers, Mr. Me-Donagh and Colonel Wood, and reads as follows:
Another matter to which our attention was drawn refers to five applications in which entitlement was recommended by the old Federal Appeal Board. The Board of Pension Commissioners took exception to the jurisdiction of that board to give entitlement in these cases. However, the judgment of the board which is in effect a judgment of a court of record, has never been set aside, and according to the record, these men should be entitled to receive the moneys awarded to them. We did not go fully into the cases as they could not be considered within the scope of our inquiry, but the attention of the government is drawn to the matter as a source of irritation making it difficult for the pension machinery to function smoothly. I submit that it is the duty of the government either to have the judgment of the Federal Appeal Board set aside if it is in fact in error, but if not, it stands as a judgment in favour of the men and should be carried out. Such irritations do more to interfere with the smooth operation of an organization than anything else that can be imagined.
Parliament is the last resort for cases such as these. The minister has refused to pay pensions in these cases, the Board of Pension Commissioners has refused to pay pensions-

I certainly have not, I have hardly begun. I desire to go through the facts in these cases and deal only with such facts as I believe to be true. I shall first give a brief resume of the case of William D. Skitch, number 43,503.
The hon. member's statement is incorrect.

I think
my hon. friend will agree that it is correct. If the statement is found not to be correct I will agree to withdraw it. I say that the minister as head of the Department of Pensions and National Health has refused to pay pensions in these cases. Skitch went overseas in October, 1915, with the 50th battalion from the city of Calgary. He arrived in France in December, 1917, and was sent to hospital because of a wound in the right leg. He returned to Canada on April 29, 1919, but his wound never healed and he died in September, 1921. He was survived by a widow and one son born on June 20, 1920. He received a pension from the date of his discharge from the army up until the time of his death. In 1922 his widow applied for a pension which was refused by the Board of Pension Commissioners. Her appeal came before the federal appeal board, the old board in operation before the new organization was consummated in 1926, and entitlement was considered on that occasion. The pension board refused to pay the pension upon the ground that the federal appeal board had exceeded its jurisdiction in dealing with the case. This particular case came before the parliamentary committee which sat in 1928 to revise the Pension Act. Many hon. members will remember that a reference was made to the Exchequer Court of Canada upon the question of jurisdiction, that is, decide whether or not the federal appeal board had proper jurisdiction to hear this appeal in the manner in which it was heard. The case was referred to the Exchequer Court of Canada in May, 1929, and in December, 1930, the Minister of Pensions and National Health applied to the Exchequer Court of Canada to withdraw the reference which had been made in 1929. I believe the reason for that, although the minister may be able to explain, would be the new legislation of 1930, which, as hon. members are aware, practically changed the entire basis of pension administration in the Do-

minion of Canada. In 1931 the reference was heard by the exchequer court, which held that the federal appeal board had jurisdiction to entertain and determine the appeal mentioned in the reference at the time it heard and determined the same. I trust that this is quite clear. After that decision of the Exchequer Court of Canada, application was made to the Department of Pensions and National Health for the payment of the pension which was found by the federal appeal board to be due to W. D. Skitch at the time the appeal was made.

Would the hon. member give the citation of the exchequer court?
Mr. MACKENZIE Vancouver): I shall be glad to send both reports to my hon. friend.

Dear Sir:
I am instructed to refer to your letter of the 17th ultimo, addressed to Colonel the Hon. Murray MacLaren, relative to claim for pension in this case, and to inform you that, while the judgment of the exchequer court to which you refer was to the effect that the federal appeal board had jurisdiction to deal with claims of this nature, the judgment in question made no order regarding payment.
It would appear that the only action which may be now taken in this case is for the applicant to renew her application as provided for by the 1931 amendments to the Pension Act.
May I point out as fairly as I can-and this is for a thirteen year old boy now living in Victoria, British Columbia-this wras a judgment rendered by what was at that time the ultimate tribunal in regard to pension legislation in this dominion, and a verdict was given to the widow and to the little boy who was then a baby and who is now thirteen years old. That boy has not to this day received payment of a single cent of pension, because the department or the Board of Pension Commissioners has refused to implement the decision of the federal appeal board as interpreted, if you like, by the Exchequer Court of Canada.

then that authority has been transferred from the Board of Pension Commissioners directly to the Department of Pensions and National Health, so that if the argument of the Secretary of State were sound prior to a certain time in the past, it has not been sound for some considerable time, because I suggest to him that the Department of Pensions and National Health have every possible authority to make payment of these pensions when they are due and payable and when they have been found to be due and payable and authorized by the Exchequer Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Parliament may take that view.

I am
coming to that point. We have five applicants who made their applications to what was in those days the court of first instance, namely, the Board of Pension Commissioners. That board turned them down, not, I admit, on the same ground in every case. In each case an appeal was made and in each case the court of last resort said that the pension was properly due to each of these five applicants. After that, the Board of Pension Commissioners, in most cases on the ground of a change of diagnosis, took the view that they would refuse to implement the judgment of the supreme tribunal. A reference was made to the Exchequer Court of Canada as to whether the appeal board then existing had full and ample jurisdiction to make the decision it made with regard to these cases. After that higher court made a finding with regard to these cases, the Board of Pension Commissioners, while having, I admit, power to pay pensions, refused to pay a cent of pension in these five cases.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend not admit that his present statement entirely exonerates the minister personally?

I am
coming to that. I had no intention in the world of making any reflection on the minister. I refer to the Department of Pensions and National Health. The only person to whom we can appeal in parliament is the minister responsible for that department, and I say that once the power of paying pensions was transferred from the Board of Pension Commissioners to the Department of Pensions and National Health, the minister or the department could have come to parliament. A similar course was taken this afternoon for a man named Campbell in regard to a claim he had for reparations for service on an English trawler, and we awarded in this house, with great sympathy for such a case, the sum of $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: What is the hon. member's authority for stating that the power was transferred from the board to the department?

I shall
be glad to give that. If the minister will read the evidence of Captain Hodgins at the recent investigation into the administration of the Pensions Act, I think he will find that this statement was made by several of the witnesses. I shall refer my hon. friend to the evidence given by Captain Hodgins.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There must be something more convincing than simply the statement that some witnesses gave that evidence.
Is Captain Hodgins not the official accountant of the minister's department?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Certainly.
Well, he is the man who made the statement.

The minister is asking:	What is the law? Where
is the authority in law? That is the point.

That has been part of the trouble in this matter all the way through. I am appealing on the ground of equity, on the fact that the highest tribunal then appointed by this parliament, wisely or unwisely-I am not criticizing or commenting on that at all-awarded a pension in each one of these five cases. A question was raised by the Board of Pension Commissioners in regard to the matter of jurisdiction. That question was settled by the judgments given by the exchequer court, which judgments I have cited to my hon. friend. That court held that the federal appeal board had complete jurisdiction. If my hon. friend would like me to read the evidence, it will be found that Mr. Justice Audette, who was an eminent judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada, repeatedly throughout the evidence in the inquiry, criticized the present chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners for having defied the mandate of a superior court. The trouble all along has been as to finding out who was the proper official to undertake the actual payment of these pensions when found due. That is why I am bringing the matter before parliament. I agree with the minister that any case which can be referred to the existing tribunals should not be brought before the house, because those tribunals are intended to be the functioning machinery in such matters. But these cases have already been given the judgment, the finding. My hon. friend will understand the Latin motto: Transit in rem judicatem. My hon. friend may say: Why do they not appeal again? Why does not this little boy, now thirteen years old, and the other applicants, lodge an application before the pension board again and go from them to the new tribunal and from them to the appeal court? That is the argument that is used occasionally in this evidence which I have in my hand, but I ask the Secretary of State, who is an eminent lawyer, is it a matter of equity and justice for five claimants to a pension who have had a

decision given in their favour by what was then the highest court in regard to pensions in this dominion, to be compelled to start all over again and possibly take two years to run through the whole gamut of uncertainty that lies in pension administration at the present time?

I know that it is not the proper procedure as a rule to bring up individual cases in parliament, but these particular cases are locked out from any other remedy except what can be afforded by the high court of parliament, and I feel that it is my duly to bring them to the attention of parliament. Here we have the judgment of the exchequer court, the judgment of the federal appeal court, the two references to the exchequer court, the evidence and the very strong and expressive language used by the chairmah of the Rinfret committee, Mr. Justice Audette, practically saying that it was a shame that these pensions were not paid. speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to condemn the minister by reason of-

The entire committee.

I read
the paragraph to the committee when I commenced my remarks; perhaps the hon. member was not in his seat. It is as follows:

It is
signed by four gentlemen, namely, Alexander Ross, Richard Myers, Frank G. J. McDonagh and W. C. Wood.

From the ex parte statement made by the hon. member it would appear that an injustice has been done. I have examined the reports of the exchequer court and the judgment of the president of that court. All he affirmed in the judgment was that the old federal appeal board had jurisdiction to entertain the appeal, notwithstanding the repeal of the legislation I think the hon. member will agree with me that that ds the only construction which could be placed upon the judgment.

I believe there must be something behind the whole matter which the hon. member has not set before the committee and the country. I suggest this, that the federal appeal board in excess of their duty and jurisdiction under statutory authority creating them, and by which they are bound, gave a different diagnosis of the case from that which they should have given, and it is on that account that the pension board have refused to pay the pension.
Even if my hon. friend's contention is correct, the exchequer court still held that the judgment should stand.
No, they did not say that.
Oh yes.

No; that is not a fair construction to place upon the judgment. All the Exchequer court held was that the federal appeal board had jurisdiction to hear the appeal, notwithstanding the repeal of the old legislation. The reports are here. I had to read them rather hurriedly, but I believe that is all the headnote or judgment indicate. That does not carry the matter as far as my hon. friend says it should go. The finding of the president of the exchequer court, which is to be found at page 102 of part IV of the Canadian Law Reports for 1931, is as follows:
There will be an order declaring that the pension appeal board as it existed on the date of the reference herein had jurisdiction to entertain and determine appeals from refusal of pension by the Board of Pension Commissioners.
It only went to the point of jurisdiction in hearing the appeals, not to the merits of the appeal at all.
Read the preceding paragraph.

It is very long. This is the finding and order of the court:
There will be an order declaring that the pension appeal board as it existed on the date of the reference herein had jurisdiction to entertain and determine appeals from refusal of pension by the Board of Pension Commissioners.
The finding of the court is exactly as I said it was, namely only on the question of jurisdiction and not on the merits at all.

Is that not
all that is necessary?

No; you have to go farther than that. The hon. member for West Edmonton knows very much more than the rest of us about most matters which are discussed. This is a legal problem however, and I venture to suggest he does not know anything about it.

May I read to the hon. member the part of the judgment to which he has referred:
I should very much doubt if the statute ever intended, that a judgment rendered on appeal, by the board, should be of no effect,-

-because the statutory directions which I have already mentioned were not complied with. It is perhaps unnecessary that I should go so far, because that point was not argued before me.
He finds that even if there were irregularities in regard to diagnosis, the judgmeint wa3 one which should be complied with.

The cases of Skitch, Isadore Ouellette and three others came before the committee on pensions and returned soldiers' problems on several occasions in 1928. We heard evidence, as I have no doubt the hon. member for Kingston and the minister will remember; I recall that we heard evidence in particular on the Ouellette case, which is similar to the Skitch case. I have before me a portion of the evidence as it appears at page 311 of the journals of the House of Commons for the year 1928. In that evidence I find a letter dated November 11, 1924, addressed to the Board of Pension Commissioners, and from the letter the committee will learn that this has been a long standing complaint. It is addressed to the Deputy Minister of Justice, and is as follows:
Dear Sir:
I have had under consideration the questions regarding the jurisdiction of the federal appeal board submitted with your letter of the seventeenth September, ultimo, and beg to advise you as follows:
In this ease it appears that the difference of opinion between the two bodies

That is, between the Board of Pension Commissioners and the federal appeal board.
-relates to a matter of diagnosis and not to the question whether the disability, if any, was attributable to military service. The Board of Pension Commissioners found that the "error of refraction resulting in defective vision was a pre-enlistment congenital condition and was not aggravated during military service."
This is the Ouellette case.
Whereas the federal appeal board found that "the defective vision in this case is due to optic neuritis, and that the weight of evidence indicates that optic neuritis was incurred on service."
It seems clear, therefore, that the federal appeal board disposed of the case upon a different diagnosis than that upon which the Board of Pension Commissioners proceeded, and that no question of attributability within the meaning of the statute was involved. I am of opinion, therefore, that the federal appeal board did not have the jurisdiction to make the order in question.
Papers returned.
Yours truly,
W. Stuart Edwards,
Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice.
Mr. Edwards gave that opinion in 1924. That was put before the pensions committee.

Hon. members will note that the letter is dated 1924. In the 1928 hearings before the committee this matter was brought up and was the subject of much discussion. The result was that in the amendment put before and passed by the house we find the following:
Any dispute as to the jurisdiction of the board to entertain and determine appeals from refusal of pension by the commission shall be referred by the department to the exchequer court for determination.
That was the considered judgment of the committee.
That is on the question of jurisdiction.
These cases in the hands of the committee wore questions of jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Was not the reference which was made subsequently to the exchequer court confined solely to the question of jurisdiction?
It was.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Therefore if the reference was solely on the question of jurisdiction the opinion or judgment of the court must necessarily be confined to the question of jurisdiction, and not extend to the merits.

The point at issue between the Board of Pension Commissioners and the federal appeal board was one of jurisdiction. The Board of Pension Commissioners had granted a pension to Ouellette and then discontinued it. Ouellette asked to have his pension continued. The board refused. In those days there was a federal appeal board; the case came before that board and the appeal board found that he was entitled to a pension on the ground that his defective vision was due to optic neuritis, whereas the Board of Pension Commissioners said he was not entitled to pension because his defective vision was due to an error of refraction which was congenital.
Is it not a fact that the federal appeal board changed the diagnosis, and had no authority in law to do it?

That is just the point; they changed the diagnosis. Admitting they changed the diagnosis, Mr. Edwards in his letter to the committee and in his letter to the minister stated:
I am of opinion, therefore, that the federal appeal board did not have the jurisdiction to make the order in question.
There was the contention of the Board of Pension Commissioners, there was the con-

tention of the Department of Justice. That was placed before the committee. I am willing to admit now that the means we took were not the best, but we did what we thought best under the circumstances. We said: Since these two boards are in dispute as to jurisdiction, any dispute as to the jurisdiction of the board to entertain and determine appeals from refusal of pension by the commission shall be referred by the department to the exchequer court for determination. Acting on that, un-deT the law passed in 1928 this case was submitted-in 1929, if my memory serves me aright-to the exchequer court; and the exchequer court decided as my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) has pointed out, and as my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has admitted. In December, 1931, the reference was heard by the exchequer court, which held that the federal appeal board had jurisdiction to entertain and determine the appeal mentioned in the reference at the time it heard and determined the same. Therefore the Board of Pension Commissioners should have granted that pension. That is, the contention of the Board of Pension Commissioners was set aside.

No, I
think that is a non sequitur. The concluding clause of the headnote reads:
That whether or not the appeal board in giving its decision complied with the statute did not go to the question of jurisdiction.
Now the Justice department, as I understand, have ruled-
May I ask when the Justice department gave a ruling?
The Justice department was heard before the exchequer court on the point and its contention was not sustained.

No, that
is not correct. That was not argued, and any remarks the judge made on that point are obiter dicta. The judge was asked only to decide the bald question of jurisdiction, and he decided that in favour of the pensioner. I think he was right. The mere fact that the statute had been repealed did not rob the federal appeal board of jurisdiction at the time when the matter was before them. I think that is sound. But it does appear from the finding of the exchequer court that the federal appeal board in giving its decision did not comply with the statute-that is the inference-on the merits. They had no right to change the diagnosis.
They did have jurisdiction?

They had jurisdiction to hear the appeal; that has been decided as a matter of record in the court. But they had no authority to change the diagnosis. I am not defending the case; I am just trying to elaborate it.

Mr. Justice Audette, the chairman of the committee in the recent investigation, referring to these cases, said:
There seems to be something wrong there. If there are two tribunals, one of the first instance and the other an appellate division, and the appellate division gives its judgment, then it is no business of the court of first instance to criticize the judgment and say, that you are not to put that into force. There must be some remedy somewhere.
Again:
Then the Minister of Pensions and National Health applied ex parte in the exchequer court, representing to the court that new tribunals had been created-
By legislation of 1930.
[DOT]-for disposing of pension decisions and asking that the reference be withdrawn. The submission was made ex parte to the president of the court-
My hon. friend has the reference.
-and he said-We have already here before us a statement of claim from the Skitch dependents and we think their solicitor should he advised of this action. Notice was accordingly given to the solicitor and we apeared before the court. There was a full dress debate on the thing. The justice department was represented, and after an argument lasting all day the president of the exchequer court came to the conclusion that the references should not be withdrawn, that there was a vested and legal right in the people who had obtained judgments from the old appeal board, and that these rights had not been cancelled by the repeal of the sections which had created the federal appeal board.
Could anything be more specific? He said there was a vested and a legal right in the people who had obtained judgment from the old board, and this could not be destroyed by the legislation amending the appeal board system passed by this house in 1930. Mr. Justice Audette also said the tribunal below had no right to question the judgment of the tribunal above. That is the situation. It is really an impasse; no one would pay these pensions. A properly constituted court found in favour of the appellants, and some of them have been waiting now eleven or twelve years without a cent of pension. There is an obvious inequity in the whole situation, and I

think it should be remedied. I am speaking entirely on the facts, not laying any blame on the minister. I would without any hesitation -lay blame on the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners.

I do not believe that a board has the right to refuse to pay a man a pension which a superior tribunal is of the opinion is properly payable. I do not think that is at all right.

The

If there is a statement from the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners, it seems to me that we should have a statement from the other side, because this matter has been hanging fire for five or six years. I will not enter into an attack on Colonel John Thompson, with whom I have been on the friendliest terms, although we have not been able to agree in this matter, but I think he will admit that ever since this case has been before the public and those interested in pensions he has repeatedly taken the position that he would not pay this pension. I have here the evidence which was given in 1928 in the Ouellette case. Colonel Belton: I may say that I am purposely avoiding mentioning names, but they may be mentioned, if you desire.

I am convinced from a review of the medical opinion available, that the defective vision in this case is due to an optic neuritis and that the weight of evidence indicates that optic neuritis was incurred on service.
The appeal is allowed.
That judgment was given in 1924. The exchequer court declared that this federal appeal board had jurisdiction to give such a judgment, yet these cases have been waiting since 1924 for final decision.
They are waiting to hear the appeal.

I will admit that the hon.
member is right-I do not believe it, but I will admit that he is right to please him.
Did the hon. member read that pension had been originally granted on account of optic neuritis?
No.
Hold on. Will the hon. gentleman please keep quiet? He is not running the whole committee.

I will read the statement
again for the information of the hon. member. This statement was made by Colonel Belton, who was chairman of the federal appeal board.
He says:
This man Ouelette had been on pension for some years, from 1919 up to April, 1923, for defective vision, due to optic neuritis.
I do not know what it was due to; I am not a medical man.

Then they cancelled the pension on the ground that it was not optic neuritis but that it was an error of refraction.
In other words, they changed the diagnosis.

The Board of Pension Commissioners, after having given him a pension for optic neuritis, said that it was an error of refraction. He went before the federal appeal board and they called in their own doctors, including Doctor Minnes and a number of other medical men from Quebec, and they said they were convinced that defective vision was due to optic neuritis, which was incurred on service. But that is not all. Let me continue the statement made by Colonel Belton:
The Board of Pension Commissioners, according to the statute-
That is, as it existed in 1928.
-had then a month during which they might appeal this decision to a quorum of the board.
Members of the house who were members of that committee will recall that there was a sort of board to which you could appeal decisions of the federal appeal board. To continue:
That was not done, but our board was advised that they considered we had gone outside of our jurisdiction in the case, and that they did not intend to carry out the recommendation for pension.

That was the attitude which Colonel Thompson took-that he would not pay the pension, no matter what you did. And the committee in its wisdom tried to do the best it could to settle the case by having it referred to the exchequer court. It was referred to the exchequer court and apparently Colonel Thompson persists in his view that no matter what court gives these poor devils a pension they will not get it. I say, Mr. Chairman, it is time that something was done in this matter. This afternoon we could give a man named Campbell some consideration-a man who had seen no service at all either in Canada or in the empire, but who had been on a trawler. He was caught on a trawler and taken to Germany and he found that he would have been entitled to place his case before the British authorities at the proper time and that he would have been entitled to some compensation under reparations. Apparently he had been in Australia. He finally drifted into Canada. He made application to the British board from Canada but was told he had no right to compensation. Out of the generosity of our hearts we said that this Englishman who, having served on a trawler, was not a soldier, should receive a pension because he happened to be loafing in Canada and Australia. He could not obtain a pension before his own courts but we out of our generosity said we would give him one. Yet every court except the Board of Pension Commissioners that has to deal with these cases has granted a pension to these men and still they cannot get it. If there is no other way of granting a pension to these men, I submit that the minister should bring in a compassionate grant.
In answer to the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), I should like to quote further from the evidence given before the commission as follows:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Well, you had no right to criticize the reasons which prompted them to arrive at the conclusion they did.
Colonel Thompson: The justice department said we had.

I do not care. The court is there duly constituted. It is not for the inferior court to say, I am not obeying the judgment because I don't think you are right. If the administration of justice was constituted that way it would be a farce.

Colonel Thompson: But surely, sir, they must act within their limited jurisdiction. That does not apply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, they did act within their jurisdiction. There was an appeal, and if you thought that the judgment was not right you could have taken it further; but it is not in your mouth to say that you are not going to obey the judgment. I think that with a little common sense and willingness, and with a heart, these cases could be brought before the department and dealt with just the same as any good businessman would deal with them. We are fighting over nothing, we are just fighting in the air; we are just standing on technicalities; you won't approach the question. It is a pretty bad example to give to the rest of Canada.

I am not a lawyer so I cannot discuss this case from the legal aspect. From what I remember of the case, it seems that the diagnosis was changed by the Board of Pension Commissioners. I do not know that they have the authority to change a diagnosis any more than anybody else. The statute says distinctly that a diagnosis must not be changed. I admit that but we organized these two boards and gave them medical men as advisers and permission to obtain other advice in connection with oases. The matter of changing a diagnosis does not come before the federal board, but in this case the Board of Pension Commissioners changed the diagnosis. I know of a concrete case where an ex-service man dropped dead in Rochester. The diagnosis was given as pneumonia. The man had been working on a ladder and when an examination was afterwards made it was found that although he had some congestion of the lungs he had also half a dozen other pathological conditions any one of which could have caused his death. The stand was taken that the diagnosis could not be changed. If the diagnosis could not be changed in that case, what right had the Board of Pension Commissioners to change another diagnosis? I am not discussing this case from the legal aspect but more along medical lines.

I should like to inquire of the minister what the practice is with regard to the admission to hospital of an ex-service man applying for pension who has established by his own medical officer, at least to some extent, that he has a disability but is told that he must have some sort of technical examination. In the particular case I have in mind a cystoscopic and X-ray examination was necessary. Application was made to put this man into hospital but it was turned down, I understand upon the ground that the Board of Pension Commissioners did not consider him entitled to pension. He was told that he would have to have this examination before

I am quite willing to be considered wrong by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is the hon. member's impatience again.
I am doing the talking now, and I shall carry on with my job. If the minister does his job equally well, there will be no complaint.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I thought the hon. member had finished.

I am only starting. It is useless for the minister to tell us that he is going to review these cases, because I know where he will go for his information. He will go to the Board of Pension Commissioners, and this board has made uip its mind that these men are not going to be paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The hon. member is wrong again.

The boat'd have said so repeatedly; they have taken advantage of every technical point they could raise. The whole thing was started by a technical point raised by Colonel Thompson in the first place. He did not like to have a court over him. He was practically told so by Judge Audette in the recent investigation.
Mr. MoGIBBON: The tribunals were over him.

They were over him. These are federal appeal board cases, and if I understood the implication of my hon. friend the tribunals are not going to be over him much longer. In any case I think the minister should give us the assurance that he will personally study these cases and if he finds there is merit in them and that he cannot under the act-perhaps he will find that under the act, no matter how much he reviews them, he cannot grant a pension-do justice in these cases, he will come before parliament with a vote in order to settle these claims once for all, to remove from the department and from the people of Canada the stigma under which they have so long been labouring. I think that is a pledge which the minister ought to give us.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
May I interject one or
two observations? I have listened with interest and close attention to the presentation of these cases, and presented as they have been they are a serious and an interesting problem. I detected, however, as we proceeded, that there were one or two points which might be possible grounds for the Board of Pension Commissioners refusing to pay. I certainly, with what information we have before us, am not in a position to express definitely an opinion whether they were right or wrong, but I submit to my hon. friends that the minister's suggestion that the matter will again be reviewed by him should be accepted in good faith. I am quite certain that he makes it in good faith, and obviously he could not in his position as minister of the department pledge himself offhand to the payment of a pension apart from the technical provisions of the law. But if the minister after reviewing the cases is convinced that there are sound grounds for special treatment, he would then have to bring them before his colleagues in council and submit to parliament whatever action might be decided upon So I think my hon. friend in his enthusiasm for these cases, which I do not call in question for one moment, is hardly fair in asking the minister to give a definite promise.
I do not want that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I personally must confess that I should want to know something more than we have been able to gather tonight before I could be clear in my own mind. Two or three points have occurred to me on which I think there is need for further light. We cannot get it here, and so I shall not mention them. The minister has not all his records here and was not prepared to deal with these cases. So I think my hon. friends should accept the minister's offer to review the oases and undoubtedly discuss them with his colleagues, and then at a future time, when the other estimates are up, the whole matter can be discussed again.

I would be satisfied if the
minister wrould say that he would review the cases and if he finds that they cannot be conveniently settled otherwise than by presenting a special bill to parliament or a special item in the estimates-by that I mean that he will not ask these poor unfortunate people to go dragging their cases again through the

whole gamut of pension board, pension tribunal, and pension appeal court-if be finds that these cases have the merit which we have urged here and which has been urged by other hon. gentlemen, all I am asking is that he will take it on himself to ask parliament as the court of last resort to pass on the matter. But if he only reviews the matter, we shall not get anywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is scarcely fair to ask
for a pledge of that kind. The minister can only say now that he will review it because he does not know until he does reivew it what conclusion he will come to.

I am
willing to accept the suggestion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that before the estimates are finally through we may expect to hear something further about these cases.

Do the salaries for the
pension tribunals come under this vote, Mr. Chairman?
No. This item applies to the Board of Pension Commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There is a special item
for the tribunals, No. 204.

The cases which have
been reviewed by my friends to my left are similar to a great many cases which no doubt can be found right across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I could cite many such cases in my own riding, and what I particularly want to point out is the unfairness of the way in which the cases are handled by the attorney or advocate who follows the pension tribunal around. Last fall in my home town a pension was awarded by the tribunal to two men-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that this matter comes under the item before us.

We shall reach the pension tribunal
item later; it is No. 204.
speakername: Mr.   Hanson-York-Sun-bury@Deputy Speaker and Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
May I say, Mr. Chairman,
that the Board of Pension Commissioners has working under it commission counsel who appeal cases from the tribunal to the appeal court, and as they are under the control of the Board of Pension Commissioners I think that any case that comes before the tribunal can properly be discussed under this item.
tMr. Power.]

I should like to refer to one remark that was made by the minister to-night. He said that these cases were all reviewed by independent bodies. I would ask the minister on whose authority does this attorney or advocate follow the tribunal around and after the men have been awarded a pension take that pension away?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
He works under the
Board of Pension Commissioners.

Then all I now say is
that we shall have more to say about this when the time comes.
Are we still on the item for the Board of Pension Commissioners, Mr. Chairman?
Yes, item 81.

Does the minister feel
that he ought to press this item, and item 204 which the Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned, when there is overhanging this parliament the idea of a new Pension Act? I submit that it is not quite fair to vote these salaries and these amounts for the various tribunals when we have had in the last six months a pensions investigation and reports varying in effect from three or four different groups of members of that committee. I do not think we ought to go on discussing these items. Does the minister think that we shall really make time by pressing these items in view of the fact that this very item is a vote for the salaries of one of the bodies which is being considered in connection with any new legislation which is being brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth was not in the house when it was agreed to allow item No. SO to stand after a certain amount of discussion until after the amendments to the Pension Act were before the house.

I was told that, and I
was suggesting that the same thing be done in connection with this item. It seems to me that we cannot go on voting money for pension administration when you are talking about radically amending pension legislation, and when you have had a pension investigation which has been reported on four different ways by four different groups of the committee that made the inquiry. I do not think parliament ought to vote these items now in view of the fact that we are going to

have legislation which may materially alter the present situation. There may be no Board of Pension Commissioners when we get through with the new legislation, or it may be that the board will be twice or three times its present size, and altogether differently constituted.

It is
understood that legislation will be introduced which may alter the three courts now functioning in regard to veteran treatment. In this connection I support the remarks of the hon. member who has just spoken. It is possible, almost probable, that the legislation may affect the size and personnel of the present Board of Pension Commissioners. When we come to the pensions tribunal it is possible that it may be abolished. How, then, can we intelligently vote appropriations at this time? How can we vote intelligently without first having before us the proposed new legislation? Surely we should not be asked to vote in the dark, and blindly to deal with an estimate based upon last year's figures until we know what the plans of the government are in regard to pensions legislation for the next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not believe I have asked the committee to vote blindly. The hon. member who has just sat down has spoken a great deal; whether it has been blindly or not I must leave to the judgment of the committee. At the same time I am quite prepared to allow the matter to stand.

I should like to ask hon. members opposite if they would be willing to vote that this item be deleted from the estimates?
Item stands.

speechtext: National defence-salaries, $441,378; contingencies, $35,000.
What is the present strength of the non-permanent forces?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. M. SUTHERLAND (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: This is a civil government item; the question of the hon. member cannot properly be asked at this point.
Perhaps the minister could answer the question. Could he give me the figures for the permanent and non-permanent forces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: On January 31 there were 3,524 in the permanent force.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Non-permanent active militia, $1,994,000.
What are the plans for training next year? I refer to the number of days training, and the number of men who train.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Generally speaking, there will be a ten day training period for about 30,000 men. For specialists such as signallers there may be a twelve day training period.
What about camps?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There will be no camps, in the general sense of the word as it was understood some years ago. There will probably be smaller camps used over a few week ends. With that exception, however, there will be no large camps.
What about Petawawa?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There will be an artillery camp at Petawawa.
Would the minister explain the increase of $111,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The increase of $111,000 is made up of grants for training. There was artillery which in the year 1931-32 had no camp training at all. Last summer a very small number of batteries went to Petawawa. During the coming summer, however, it is felt that there will have to be a larger quota go to Petawawa in order to keep up efficiency. That accounts for the greater part of the increase. Then, as I have said, there will be a little more training for specialists, such as machine gunners and signallers.
Was there any training at Valcartier last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: A number of regiments in that dstrict took the funds they were given for training purposes and used them for short training periods of three or four days each.

I am talking about rural units. Is it the intention of the government this year to have them train locally, or does the minister intend to have a quota of officers go to Valcartier for training?

Does the minister intend to carry on the same kind of training this year so far as non-commissioned officers and officers are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The whole object of the training is to train the key men, namely the officers and the non-commissioned officers.
There will be no local camps at local headquarters so far as whole regiments are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.

The minister kindly explained how the increased amount was to be expended. I understood him to say it was in additional field artillery training. Why under existing economic conditions does he consider it advisable to increase the vote for artillery training this year by $111,000? Is there anything ahead of us that we must fear? Are we going to be attacked in the near future, or is he going to send a force away somewhere? We got along all right last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The vote as a whole is down, but this vote for the non-permanent militia is really the key vote of the whole department. Everything else hinges on it, because if anything ever did happen it is the non-permanent militia which would have to be expanded to do the work. Therefore it is very important that the key people be kept on an efficient basis. It could not be kept on an efficient basis the way it has been going the last couple of years. I assure the hon. member that it is far from full battery strength; we have the lowest possible number from which we consider we can get efficient training.
Would the minister also inform us if it is the intention of the department to pay to the local regiments-I mean rural regiments especially-the ordinary allowances they are entitled to per annum?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
For the care of
arms, yes.
Item agreed to
Naval services-to provide for the maintenance of the ships and establishments of the naval service including the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve and the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, $2,422,000.
What is the reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Last year in the
vote there was an amount for preliminary work in connection with a new trawler. The naval staff have been very insistent that we needed one or two new trawlers, because the Thiepval that we had on the western coast was sunk some three years ago. This year the Ypres is out of commission; I do not think it will ever be going again. They urged that very strongly last year, and an item for preliminary expense was included. That is cut out this year and the idea given up for the time being.

It was not spent last
year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.

What is the program in
regard to naval training this year-the same as last?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Practically the same. The two destroyers on the eastern coast this year have been taking a trip in southern waters The two on the western coast went further south in the Pacific. The general plan of training is practically the same as last year.
How many boats have we?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have six boats in commission-two destroyers and one mine sweeper on each coast.
Is the bulk of this money used for salaries, or is it upkeep of the boats?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is practically all for salaries. These boats have to have a certain amount of refitting in the dry docks every year, and staffs are maintained at the dry docks for that purpose. '
What is the total personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: About 850.
How many officers and how many other ranks?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There are 89 officers; that would leave about 790 other ranks.

Could the minister tell me what the rate of pay is for the ordinary seaman? If he cannot find the information he can give it to me at some other time. I thought surely the officers would know the daily rates of pay.
They know the officers' rates.
How is the minister getting on with the Canadian personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are gradually
getting on with the personnel. At the present time we have on loan from the Royal Navy 8 officers and 66 other ranks.
May I ask the minister if there will soon be some vacant positions in the royal navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: At the present time we are not taking on any men, because the estimates have been cut, and the wastage, that is the gradual dropping out of men, is very small. Consequently there are practically no new openings.
There are only 66 men?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, the 66 are men that we have from the royal navy who have been on loan. Now I have the information as to pay: Ordinary seamen, $1.25 a day; stokers, $1.35; artificers, $2.10; artisan ratings, $2.10. Then they take on some younger boys at 60 cents a day.
For how long do these men serve?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: A seven year term.
